planting.note: Divide clumps or set out container stock in spring into gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade.

directions: A Mediterranean and Balkan woodland-edge relative of the common deadnettle, this species forms low, semi-evergreen mats of soft, hairy, toothed leaves that stay more restrained and slower-spreading than Lamium maculatum. In late spring it produces whorls of large, hooded, rosy-purple to magenta two-lipped flowers held just above the foliage. It prefers gritty, sharply draining soil and resents winter wet, making it a good fit for part-shade rock gardens or woodland-edge plantings rather than deep, damp shade. Less cold-hardy and less vigorous than its northern European cousins, it suits zone 6-9 gardens with mild, well-drained conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after frost danger passes into moist, humus-rich soil in part shade; mulch over winter in the colder end of its range.

directions: Native to the Himalayan foothills and parts of East and South Asia, this species forms flat, tight rosettes of small, often bronze-tinged leaves that creep along the soil surface by short runners. Short spikes of small blue-violet, two-lipped flowers appear above the foliage in spring. It has long been used in traditional Asian herbal preparations but is grown ornamentally in mild-winter gardens as a warm-climate, lower-growing alternative to the familiar Ajuga reptans. Best suited to zone 7-10 gardens, it tolerates less cold than common bugleweed and prefers consistent moisture with good drainage in part shade.
